cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(a): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'If the Council is deadlocked on a legislative proposal, the European Council can break the deadlock by adopting the act itself by consensus of the Heads of State or Government.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False – the European Council has no legislative function; it can only give political impetus.
• Rule: Art 15(1) TEU – the European Council defines the general political directions and priorities but 'shall not exercise legislative functions'. Legislative acts are adopted by the European Parliament and the Council (Art 14(1), 16(1) TEU; Art 289 TFEU).
• Application: an act it adopted itself would come from an institution without competence and could be annulled (Art 263(1) TFEU also covers European Council acts intended to produce legal effects).
• What it can do: give political guidance to unblock the file; where unanimity is the obstacle, let the Council switch to QMV through the general passerelle (Art 48(7) TEU: unanimity, EP consent, no national parliament objecting) – the act is still adopted by the Council with the EP.
Codex: Art 14(1), 15(1), 16(1), 48(7) TEU; Art 263(1), 289 TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(b): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'The European Parliament can force a Commissioner who is involved in a lobbying scandal to resign by adopting a motion of censure against him alone.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False – a motion of censure can only be directed against the Commission as a whole.
• Rule: the Commission is collectively responsible to the EP (Art 17(8) TEU). A motion of censure carried by two thirds of the votes cast, representing a majority of the component members (361 of 720), forces all members of the Commission to resign as a body (Art 234 TFEU).
• Individual Commissioner: only the Commission President can require a member to resign (Art 17(6) TEU); for serious misconduct the Court of Justice may compulsorily retire him on application of the Council or the Commission (Art 247 TFEU).
• Application: the EP can only express its lack of confidence in him (under the Framework Agreement the President must then request the resignation or explain the refusal) – or censure the whole college.
Codex: Art 17(6), 17(8) TEU; Art 234, 247 TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(c): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'The Council of the European Union is headed by a President elected for two and a half years, who chairs all of its meetings.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: False – this describes the President of the European Council; the presidency of the Council of the EU rotates among the Member States.
• European Council: its President is elected by the European Council by QMV for two and a half years, renewable once, and may not hold a national office (Art 15(5)–(6) TEU).
• Council of the EU: the presidency of its configurations is held by the Member State representatives on the basis of equal rotation (Art 16(9) TEU; Art 236(b) TFEU) – in practice six months each, coordinated in 18-month trios. Exception: the Foreign Affairs Council is chaired by the High Representative (Art 18(3) TEU).
• The statement therefore confuses two separate institutions (both listed in Art 13(1) TEU).
Codex: Art 13(1), 15(5)–(6), 16(9), 18(3) TEU; Art 236 TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(d): Comment on the following statement and indicate whether it is true or false. Justify your answer. 'Under the ordinary legislative procedure, an act can be adopted at first reading without the Council ever adopting a position of its own.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: True – if the Council approves the European Parliament's first-reading position, the act is adopted in that wording (Art 294(4) TFEU).
• Procedure: Commission proposal to the EP and the Council (Art 294(2)) → the EP adopts its position at first reading and communicates it to the Council (294(3)) → if the Council approves that position (QMV, Art 16(3) TEU; unanimity for EP amendments the Commission rejects, Art 293(1)), the act is adopted in the wording corresponding to the EP's position (294(4)). Only if the Council does not approve it does it adopt its own first-reading position (294(5)), and the second reading follows.
• Practice: because of informal trilogues, about 89% of OLP acts in 2014–2019 were adopted at first reading.
Codex: Art 289(1), 293(1), 294(2)–(5) TFEU; Art 16(3) TEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(a): The Commission submits to the European Parliament and the Council a proposal for a (fictitious) 'Regulation on the labelling of AI-generated images', based on Art 114 TFEU (ordinary legislative procedure). At first reading the Parliament adopts its position with 30 amendments; the Commission accepts all of them and alters its proposal accordingly. In the Council (27 Member States), 16 Member States representing 64.5% of the EU population vote to approve the Parliament's position, 4 Member States (16.0%) vote against and 7 Member States (19.5%) abstain. Has the Council approved the Parliament's position, and what happens next? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – the 65% population threshold is missed and the 11 states not voting in favour form a valid blocking minority, so the Council must now adopt its own first-reading position (Art 294(5) TFEU).
• Rule: the Council approves the EP's position by QMV (Art 16(3) TEU; Art 294(4) TFEU). Unanimity would be needed only for EP amendments the Commission rejects (Art 293(1)); here the Commission accepted all of them and altered its proposal (Art 293(2)), so QMV applies. QMV = at least 55% of the members (15 of 27) representing at least 65% of the EU population; a blocking minority must include at least four members, failing which QMV is deemed attained (Art 16(4) TEU).
• States: 16 ≥ 15 – met. Population: 64.5% < 65% – not met.
• Abstentions: in QMV only votes in favour count, so an abstention works like a 'no'. The 11 states that did not vote in favour (35.5% of the population) are more than four members → the 'deemed attained' rule does not apply → the EP's position is NOT approved.
• Next step: the Council adopts its own position at first reading and communicates it to the EP with its reasons (Art 294(5)–(6)). As the Commission's proposal now mirrors the EP's position, any different Council text amends that proposal: unanimity is required, unless the Commission agrees and alters its proposal again – then QMV suffices (Art 293(1)–(2)). No time limit applies to the first reading.
Codex: Art 16(3)–(4) TEU; Art 293, 294(3)–(6) TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(b): The Commission has proposed a (fictitious) 'Regulation on the labelling of AI-generated images' based on Art 114 TFEU (ordinary legislative procedure). The Council failed to approve the European Parliament's first-reading position. It now votes on adopting its own position at first reading, which the Commission supports. 23 Member States representing 57.9% of the EU population vote in favour; Germany, France and Poland (together 42.0%) and Luxembourg (0.1%) vote against. Is the Council's position adopted? Would the result be different if Luxembourg (i) abstained, or (ii) voted in favour? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not adopted, and a Luxembourg abstention would change nothing; but if Luxembourg voted in favour, the three remaining opponents could not block and QMV would be deemed attained.
• Rule: Art 16(4) TEU – QMV requires 55% of the members (15 of 27) and 65% of the population; 'a blocking minority must include at least four Council members, failing which the qualified majority shall be deemed attained'.
• Basic case: 23 states ≥ 15, but 57.9% < 65%. The opponents are four members with 42.1% (more than 35%) → a valid blocking minority → position NOT adopted.
• (i) Abstention: in QMV an abstention is simply not a vote in favour, so Luxembourg stays in the non-supporting group of four → still NOT adopted.
• (ii) Luxembourg votes in favour: 24 states with 58.0% – the population threshold is still missed, but only three members (DE, FR, PL) do not support the text. A blocking minority needs at least four members → QMV is deemed attained → position ADOPTED, although the three states represent 42% of the population. The rule stops the largest states from blocking on their own.
• Because the Commission supports the Council's text (it can alter its proposal accordingly, Art 293(2)), QMV is enough; without its support, departing from the Commission's proposal would need unanimity (Art 293(1) TFEU).
Codex: Art 16(3)–(4) TEU; Art 293, 294(5) TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(c): In the ordinary legislative procedure on a (fictitious) 'Regulation on the labelling of AI-generated images' (Art 114 TFEU), the Council adopts its first-reading position and communicates it to the European Parliament (all 720 seats filled) on 15 September 2027. On 6 December 2027, 352 MEPs vote in favour of a motion to reject the Council's position, 318 vote against and 30 abstain. No other vote takes place before the deadline expires. What is the result? What if 365 MEPs had voted for rejection? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The rejection fails because it needs 361 votes (a majority of the component members); as the EP takes no other decision in time, the act is deemed adopted in the wording of the Council's position. With 365 votes the act would be deemed not adopted.
• Rule: second reading, Art 294(7) TFEU – within three months (extendable by one month, Art 294(14)) the EP may (a) approve the Council's position or take no decision → act deemed adopted in the Council's wording; (b) reject it by a majority of its component members → act deemed not adopted; (c) propose amendments by a majority of its component members → the text goes back to the Council and the Commission.
• Application: a majority of component members is 361 of 720, not a majority of those voting. 352 votes beat the 318 against, but fall short of 361 → no valid rejection. The three months run until 15 December 2027 (one month longer if extended) → the EP 'has not taken a decision' → act deemed adopted (294(7)(a)); it is then signed by the Presidents of the EP and the Council and published (Art 297(1)).
• Variant: 365 ≥ 361 → valid rejection → the act is deemed not adopted (294(7)(b)); the procedure ends and a new Commission proposal would be needed.
Codex: Art 14(2) TEU; Art 231, 294(7), 294(14), 297(1) TFEU.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(d): The (fictitious) 'Regulation on the labelling of AI-generated images', adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure on the basis of Art 114 TFEU, is published in the Official Journal on 10 March 2028; it does not specify a date of entry into force. When does it enter into force? An Austrian minister wants the Nationalrat to pass a federal act copying the regulation's text 'so that it becomes valid in Austria'. Comment. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: It enters into force on 30 March 2028 and applies directly in Austria; no transposition is needed, and the Nationalrat may not re-enact it in a way that conceals its EU nature.
• Entry into force: on the date the act specifies or, failing that, on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal (Art 297(1) third subpara TFEU) → 20th day after 10 March = 30 March 2028.
• Effect: a regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States (Art 288(2) TFEU) – valid in Austria without any national act.
• Copying it is prohibited where it obscures its Union nature and the Court's jurisdiction (Variola, 34/73); Austria adopts only the accompanying measures the regulation requires (authorities, penalties).
Codex: Art 288(2), 297(1) TFEU · Case: Variola (34/73).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(a): Concerned about 'over-tourism', the Commission proposes a (fictitious) 'Directive on sustainable urban tourism' based on Art 195(2) TFEU. It would oblige all Member States to cap short-term holiday rentals at 5% of the housing stock in every city district containing a UNESCO World Heritage site. According to the explanatory memorandum, its sole aim is to preserve the character of historic city centres and residents' quality of life. What kind of competence does the Union have in this field, and can the directive be adopted on the basis of Art 195(2) TFEU? Could the Commission instead rely on Art 114 or Art 352 TFEU? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Tourism is only a supporting competence and Art 195(2) TFEU expressly excludes harmonisation; neither Art 114 nor Art 352 TFEU can be used to get round that exclusion, so the Union lacks competence.
• Conferral: the Union may act only within the competences conferred on it, and every act needs a legal basis (Art 4(1), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU). The type of competence comes from the catalogue (Art 2–6 TFEU), the legal basis from the policy chapter (Art 2(6) TFEU).
• Type: tourism is a supporting, coordinating or supplementing competence (Art 6(d) TFEU); binding acts in these areas 'shall not entail harmonisation' (Art 2(5) TFEU). Art 195(2) TFEU allows OLP measures that complement Member State action, 'excluding any harmonisation'. A uniform 5% cap in all Member States harmonises national rental law → Art 195 does not cover it. Treating the aim as cultural heritage changes nothing: culture is also a supporting competence and Art 167(5) TFEU allows only incentive measures, excluding harmonisation.
• Art 114 TFEU: the measure must genuinely aim to improve the conditions for the establishment and functioning of the internal market; mere disparities between national laws are not enough, and Art 114 may not be used to circumvent an express exclusion of harmonisation (Tobacco Advertising, C-376/98). Here the sole aim is protecting historic centres → no internal-market objective → not available.
• Art 352 TFEU: the flexibility clause (Council unanimity, EP consent) cannot entail harmonisation where the Treaties exclude it (Art 352(3)) → not available.
• Conclusion: no legal basis; if adopted, the directive could be annulled for lack of competence (Art 263(2) TFEU). The Union may only support the Member States (funding, exchange of best practice, non-binding recommendations).
Codex: Art 4(1), 5(1)–(2), 13(2) TEU; Art 2(5)–(6), 6(c)–(d), 114, 167(5), 195, 263, 352 TFEU · Case: Germany v Parliament and Council (Tobacco Advertising, C-376/98).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(b): The Commission withdrew its draft 'Directive on sustainable urban tourism' (a cap on short-term holiday rentals under Art 195(2) TFEU) and now proposes a (fictitious) regulation under Art 114 TFEU (ordinary legislative procedure) obliging online short-term rental platforms to transmit booking data to national authorities in a single EU format. Within eight weeks of its transmission, reasoned opinions claiming a breach of the principle of subsidiarity are sent by the unicameral parliaments of Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Hungary, Portugal, Malta, Greece and Latvia, by the Austrian Bundesrat and by the Dutch Eerste Kamer (Senate). Does the principle of subsidiarity apply to this proposal, and what are the consequences of the reasoned opinions? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – the internal market is a shared competence; the opinions total 18 of 54 votes, exactly one third, so a 'yellow card' is triggered: the Commission must review the draft but may maintain it.
• Applicability: subsidiarity applies in all areas outside the Union's exclusive competence (Art 5(3) TEU); the internal market is a shared competence (Art 4(2)(a) TFEU). Test: the objective cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States (necessity) and can, by reason of its scale or effects, be better achieved at Union level (added value).
• Counting (Protocol No 2, Art 7(1)): each national parliament has two votes; in a bicameral system each chamber has one. 8 unicameral parliaments × 2 = 16, + Bundesrat 1 + Eerste Kamer 1 = 18 of 54 votes.
• Yellow card (Art 7(2)): reasoned opinions representing at least one third of all votes (18) → the draft must be reviewed; the Commission may maintain, amend or withdraw it, giving reasons. No veto.
• Orange card (Art 7(3), OLP only): would need a simple majority (28 votes); the proposal could then be stopped before the end of first reading by 55% of the Council members or a majority of the votes cast in the EP – not reached here.
Codex: Art 5(3), 12(b) TEU; Art 4(2)(a), 114 TFEU; Protocol No 2, Art 6–7.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(c): A (fictitious) regulation under Art 114 TFEU obliging online short-term rental platforms to transmit booking data to national authorities in a single EU format triggered a 'yellow card' from national parliaments, but the Commission maintained it. The European Parliament and the Council adopt it unchanged under the ordinary legislative procedure, and it is published in the Official Journal on 2 May 2028. The Danish Folketing still considers that it breaches the principle of subsidiarity. How can the matter be brought before the Court, and by when? Could the Committee of the Regions bring a similar action? How intensively will the Court review subsidiarity? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Denmark brings – or notifies on behalf of the Folketing – an action for annulment before the Court of Justice by 26 July 2028; the Committee of the Regions has no standing here, and the Court's review is limited.
• Basis: Art 8 Protocol No 2 – actions under Art 263 TFEU for infringement of subsidiarity are brought by Member States or notified by them, in accordance with their legal order, on behalf of their national parliament or a chamber of it. The Folketing cannot sue itself; Denmark is the (privileged) applicant (Art 263(2)), and the Court of Justice, not the General Court, decides (Art 51 Statute: Member State against a legislative act). In its own name Denmark may also plead other grounds.
• Time limit: two months (Art 263(6) TFEU), counted from the end of the 14th day after publication (16 May), plus 10 days on account of distance (Art 50–51 Rules of Procedure of the Court of Justice) → 16 July + 10 days = 26 July 2028 (a Wednesday).
• Committee of the Regions: may sue only against legislative acts for which the TFEU requires its consultation (Art 8 second paragraph Protocol No 2); Art 114 TFEU requires consultation of the Economic and Social Committee only → no standing.
• Review: the Court checks whether the legislature gave reasons on subsidiarity (implicit reasons may suffice, Germany v Parliament and Council, C-233/94) and could reasonably find that the aim is better achieved at Union level (Alliance for Natural Health, C-154/04 and C-155/04); no act has so far been annulled on this ground.
Codex: Art 5(3) TEU; Art 114, 256(1), 263(2), 263(6) TFEU; Protocol No 2, Art 8; Statute of the Court, Art 51 · not in the codex: Rules of Procedure of the Court of Justice, Art 49–51 · Cases: Germany v Parliament and Council (C-233/94), Alliance for Natural Health (C-154/04 and C-155/04).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(a): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a brewery established in Czechia, lawfully brews and sells in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'. Since 2027 the Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH has been selling the lager in Austrian supermarkets and petrol-station shops. The (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act provides: § 3 – a drink may be marketed under the name 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer, whatever its origin, may be sold at petrol stations. Austrian breweries traditionally brew in line with § 3. Assume that EU secondary law harmonises neither beer designations nor the places where beer may be sold. A Lower Austrian district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 for selling the lager as 'Bier' and for selling beer at petrol stations. Austria argues that consumers expect 'Bier' to meet the traditional purity standard, that rice-based beer is less healthy, and that § 7 prevents drink-driving. Which fundamental freedom is affected, where is it regulated, and does its scope apply? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The free movement of goods (Art 28 and 34 TFEU, justification in Art 36 TFEU); its scope applies because beer is a good imported from another Member State and the matter is not harmonised.
• Material scope: goods are products that have a monetary value and can be the subject of commercial transactions (Commission v Italy, 7/68) – beer qualifies. Art 28(2): products originating in the Member States (and third-country products in free circulation).
• Cross-border element: the lager is produced in Czechia and imported into Austria. That the importer Hopfenhandel is an Austrian company does not matter – the freedom attaches to the goods.
• Addressee: Art 34 binds the Member States, i.e. all public authorities – here the Austrian legislature and the district authority.
• No exhaustive harmonisation (assumed) → the national rules are tested directly against Art 34–36 TFEU. Art 30 and 110 TFEU are irrelevant (no customs duty or tax).
• Art 34 has direct effect (Iannelli & Volpe, 74/76), so Hopfenhandel can rely on it against the fine.
Codex: Art 26, 28, 34, 36 TFEU · Cases: Commission v Italy (7/68), Iannelli & Volpe (74/76).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(b): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a brewery established in Czechia, lawfully brews and sells in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'. Since 2027 the Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH has been selling the lager in Austrian supermarkets and petrol-station shops. The (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act provides: § 3 – a drink may be marketed under the name 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer, whatever its origin, may be sold at petrol stations. Austrian breweries traditionally brew in line with § 3. Assume that EU secondary law harmonises neither beer designations nor the places where beer may be sold. A Lower Austrian district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 for selling the lager as 'Bier' and for selling beer at petrol stations. Austria argues that consumers expect 'Bier' to meet the traditional purity standard, that rice-based beer is less healthy, and that § 7 prevents drink-driving. Does § 3 of the Beer Act restrict the free movement of goods? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – § 3 is a product requirement and therefore a measure having equivalent effect to a quantitative restriction (MEEQR) under Art 34 TFEU, even though it applies to Austrian and imported beer alike.
• § 3 is not a quota, so the question is whether it is an MEEQR. Dassonville (8/74): all trading rules of the Member States capable of hindering, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially, intra-Union trade.
• Cassis de Dijon (120/78): rules on the requirements goods must meet (composition, designation, labelling) are MEEQRs even if they apply without distinction, because imported goods lawfully made under home-state rules must be adapted – a dual burden.
• Application: Lipa must either change its recipe for Austria or give up the name 'Bier' and adapt its labels and marketing; Austrian breweries already comply → access of the Czech beer to the Austrian market is hindered – the situation of the German beer purity law (Commission v Germany, 178/84).
• Keck does not help: § 3 concerns the product itself (name and ingredients), not a selling arrangement.
• Mutual recognition: a product lawfully produced and marketed in one Member State is presumed admissible in the others unless the host state justifies the obstacle (now Reg (EU) 2019/515).
Codex: Art 34 TFEU; Reg (EU) 2019/515 · Cases: Dassonville (8/74), Cassis de Dijon (120/78), Keck (C-267/91 and C-268/91), Commission v Germany (beer purity, 178/84).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(c): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a brewery established in Czechia, lawfully brews and sells in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'. Since 2027 the Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH has been selling the lager in Austrian supermarkets and petrol-station shops. The (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act provides: § 3 – a drink may be marketed under the name 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer, whatever its origin, may be sold at petrol stations. Austrian breweries traditionally brew in line with § 3. Assume that EU secondary law harmonises neither beer designations nor the places where beer may be sold. A Lower Austrian district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 for selling the lager as 'Bier' and for selling beer at petrol stations. Austria argues that consumers expect 'Bier' to meet the traditional purity standard, that rice-based beer is less healthy, and that § 7 prevents drink-driving. Assuming that § 3 restricts the free movement of goods, can Austria justify it? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – consumers can be protected by labelling, and the health argument is unproven and incoherent, so § 3 is disproportionate and infringes Art 34 TFEU in so far as it applies to beer lawfully produced in other Member States.
• Grounds: § 3 applies without distinction, so Austria may invoke both the written grounds of Art 36 TFEU (here: protection of human health) and the unwritten mandatory requirements of Cassis de Dijon (here: consumer protection, which is NOT listed in Art 36). Purely economic aims, such as shielding domestic breweries, never justify a restriction (settled case law), and the measure must not be a disguised restriction on trade (Art 36, second sentence).
• Consumer protection: a legitimate aim, but § 3 is not necessary. Consumers can be informed by compulsory labelling of the ingredients (e.g. 'brewed with rice'), which restricts trade far less. 'Bier' is a generic designation, and national law may not crystallise consumer habits so as to secure an advantage for domestic producers (Commission v Germany, beer purity, 178/84).
• Health (Art 36): Member States may choose their level of protection, but must show a real risk on the basis of scientific evidence – rice is an ordinary foodstuff. Moreover, § 3 does not keep the drink off the market (it may still be sold under another name), so it is not even suitable to protect health: the aim is not pursued consistently.
• Burden of proof: on Austria, which must show that no less restrictive means would be equally effective.
• Conclusion: not justified → § 3 may not be applied to imported beer, and the fine is unlawful to that extent. (Applying § 3 to Austrian breweries is a purely internal situation; such reverse discrimination is not caught by Art 34.)
Codex: Art 34, 36 TFEU · Cases: Cassis de Dijon (120/78), Commission v Germany (beer purity, 178/84).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(d): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a brewery established in Czechia, lawfully brews and sells in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'. Since 2027 the Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH has been selling the lager in Austrian supermarkets and petrol-station shops. The (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act provides: § 3 – a drink may be marketed under the name 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer, whatever its origin, may be sold at petrol stations. Austrian breweries traditionally brew in line with § 3. Assume that EU secondary law harmonises neither beer designations nor the places where beer may be sold. A Lower Austrian district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 for selling the lager as 'Bier' and for selling beer at petrol stations. Austria argues that consumers expect 'Bier' to meet the traditional purity standard, that rice-based beer is less healthy, and that § 7 prevents drink-driving. Assess § 7 (the ban on selling beer at petrol stations) under the free movement of goods. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: § 7 is a selling arrangement within the meaning of Keck which, on the facts, applies to all traders and affects domestic and imported beer in the same way; it therefore falls outside Art 34 TFEU, and the fine for the petrol-station sales is compatible with EU law.
• Keck (C-267/91 and C-268/91): national rules restricting or prohibiting certain selling arrangements (where, when and by whom goods are sold) are not MEEQRs, provided they (1) apply to all relevant traders operating within the national territory and (2) affect in the same manner, in law and in fact, the marketing of domestic products and of those from other Member States.
• Application: § 7 regulates where beer may be sold, not the product itself. It applies to all sellers and all beer; Austrian beer is equally banned from petrol stations, and Lipa's lager can still be sold in supermarkets → no sign of an unequal burden in fact. Compare the sale of processed baby milk only in pharmacies (Commission v Greece, C-391/92).
• Variant: if the ban in fact hit imports harder (e.g. because petrol stations were the only realistic route to market for new foreign brands), it would be an MEEQR (Gourmet, C-405/98) – but likely justified under Art 36 TFEU (protection of human life and health: preventing drink-driving), provided it is proportionate.
Codex: Art 34, 36 TFEU · Cases: Keck and Mithouard (C-267/91 and C-268/91), Commission v Greece (C-391/92), Gourmet International (C-405/98).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(e): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a brewery established in Czechia, lawfully brews and sells in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier'. The Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH sells it in Austria. The (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act provides: § 3 – a drink may be marketed under the name 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 – no beer, whatever its origin, may be sold at petrol stations. A Lower Austrian district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 for selling the lager as 'Bier' and for selling beer at petrol stations. Hopfenhandel appeals against the fine to the Landesverwaltungsgericht Niederösterreich (regional administrative court), whose decisions can be challenged by revision before the Verwaltungsgerichtshof. It asks the court 'to send the case to Luxembourg so that the Court of Justice annuls the Austrian Beer Act'. May or must the court refer, is it bound by Hopfenhandel's request, and what can the Court of Justice do? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The court may, but need not, refer a question on the interpretation of Art 34 and 36 TFEU; Hopfenhandel cannot compel a reference, and the Court of Justice will not annul the Beer Act but only interpret EU law.
• Court or tribunal (Art 267 TFEU): established by law, permanent, independent, compulsory jurisdiction, inter partes procedure, applies rules of law (Vaassen, 61/65) – an Austrian administrative court qualifies. The question concerns the interpretation of the Treaties (Art 267(1)(a)) and is needed to decide on the fine (Art 267(2)).
• Right, not duty: its decisions can be challenged before the Verwaltungsgerichtshof → it may refer (Art 267(2)). Only a court of last instance must refer (Art 267(3)) – here the Verwaltungsgerichtshof, subject to the CILFIT exceptions (283/81); Commission v Germany (178/84) may already make the answer clear (acte éclairé, whatever the type of the earlier proceedings).
• No party right: referring is the national court's sole decision; the parties can only suggest it.
• Role of the Court: it does not annul or interpret national law in a reference; it reformulates the question ('Must Art 34 and 36 TFEU be interpreted as precluding national legislation such as …?') and leaves the application to the national court. Annulment (Art 263 TFEU) exists only for EU acts; Austria can be sued only by the Commission or another Member State (Art 258–259 TFEU).
Codex: Art 19(3)(b) TEU; Art 258, 259, 263, 267 TFEU · Cases: Vaassen (61/65), CILFIT (283/81), Commission v Germany (178/84).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 4(f): Case exercise. Pivovar Lipa s.r.o., a Czech brewery, lawfully brews in Czechia a lager made from barley malt with 20% rice, labelled 'Lipa – Bier', which the Austrian importer Hopfenhandel GmbH sells in Austria. Under § 3 of the (fictitious) Austrian Beer Act, a drink may be marketed as 'Bier' only if it is brewed exclusively from barley malt, hops, yeast and water; § 7 bans the sale of any beer at petrol stations. A district authority fines Hopfenhandel €5,000 under both provisions. Hopfenhandel appeals to the Landesverwaltungsgericht Niederösterreich, which refers a question to the Court of Justice. The Court rules that Art 34 and 36 TFEU preclude national legislation such as § 3. What must the Landesverwaltungsgericht now do, and what does the ruling mean beyond this case? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: It must disapply § 3 of its own motion and annul the fine in so far as it rests on § 3; beyond the case, the interpretation binds all Austrian courts and authorities.
• Binding effect and primacy: the ruling binds the referring court (and any appeal court in the same case), which must set aside the conflicting national provision itself, without waiting for the legislature or the Verfassungsgerichtshof (Costa v ENEL, 6/64; Simmenthal, 106/77). The part of the fine based on § 7 can stand (a Keck selling arrangement).
• Beyond the case: the interpretation applies de facto erga omnes and ex tunc; all courts and authorities must disapply § 3 for imported beer (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88), and Austria must amend its law (Art 4(3) TEU) or face infringement proceedings (Art 258 TFEU).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 34, 258, 267 TFEU · Cases: Costa v ENEL (6/64), Simmenthal (106/77), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88).
